title: Cliff Booth Returns: Brad Pitt’s Wild New Adventure Reviewed by The Hollywood Reporter
body:
Brad Pitt returns to the sun‑splashed streets of 1970s Los Angeles in Netflix’s new limited series “The Further Mis‑Adventures of Cliff Booth,” a glossy, genre‑bending homage that expands the world of Quentin Tarentino’s “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” The eight‑part saga follows the eponymous stuntman, now a reluctant private‑eye, as he navigates a city teetering between gritty realism and psychedelic excess. Pitt’s effortless charisma anchors a cast that includes Elizabeth Debicki as a mysterious femme‑fatale, Scott Caan as a hard‑boiled detective, Carla Gugino as a seasoned Hollywood insider, and Yah‑Ya Abdul‑Mateen II as a charismatic record‑label exec. Together they paint a vivid portrait of a bygone era while delivering fresh twists that keep the story moving beyond its predecessor.

From the opening notes of Boz Scaggs’ “Lowdown,” the series sets a tone that feels both nostalgic and contemporary. The choice of the mellow yacht‑rock anthem—its laid‑back groove echoing the languid heat of a California summer—signals the show’s intent to blend reverence with reinvention. Visually, the production spares no expense: saturated color palettes, period‑accurate set pieces, and a soundtrack that weaves together classic rock, funk, and early disco. These details do more than decorate; they serve as narrative signposts, guiding viewers through a Los Angeles that is simultaneously familiar and mythologized.

Pitt’s performance marks a notable evolution from his earlier cameo as the stoic, silent partner to Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton. Here, Cliff Booth is given room to speak, think, and, crucially, doubt. The series explores his post‑Hollywood life, revealing a man haunted by his past exploits and the moral ambiguities of the stunt industry. His investigative arc—probing a missing‑person case that spirals into a larger conspiracy involving music moguls, corrupt police, and the nascent drug trade—allows the actor to showcase a broader emotional range. While still delivering the effortless cool that defined his earlier portrayal, Pitt also injects vulnerability, particularly in scenes with Debicki’s enigmatic character, whose motives remain tantalizingly opaque.

The supporting ensemble adds depth and texture to the narrative. Debicki’s portrayal of a former model turned record‑label executive is a study in power dynamics, reflecting the shifting roles of women in the entertainment business during the late ’70s. Her chemistry with Pitt crackles, oscillating between flirtation and rivalry, and provides the series’ emotional core. Caan, as a grizzled LAPD detective, brings a grounded, procedural sensibility that anchors the more flamboyant elements of the plot. Meanwhile, Gugino’s cameo as a veteran Hollywood publicist offers a meta‑commentary on the industry’s self‑obsession, and Abdul‑Mateen II’s charismatic presence as a rising music impresario underscores the era’s cultural cross‑pollination between film and music.

Critics have praised the series for its meticulous production design and its willingness to expand the universe Tarantino introduced without simply rehashing familiar beats. The show’s writers have deliberately infused the storyline with period‑specific social issues—such as the rise of gang violence, the early stirrings of the LGBTQ rights movement, and the exploitation of stunt performers—to give the narrative a contemporary relevance. By juxtaposing Booth’s personal journey with these broader themes, the series invites viewers to reconsider the mythic veneer of Hollywood’s golden age.

Looking ahead, “The Further Mis‑Adventures of Cliff Booth” positions itself as a springboard for further explorations of Tarantino‑inspired characters, potentially paving the way for spin‑offs that delve into other peripheral figures from the original film. With its blend of stylish nostalgia, strong performances, and a willingness to interrogate the darker undercurrents of 1970s Los Angeles, the series is likely to resonate with both fans of the original movie and newcomers drawn to high‑quality period drama. As Netflix continues to invest in prestige television, the success of this limited run may signal a resurgence of cinematic universes that thrive on character‑driven storytelling rather than blockbuster spectacle.
